public_rationale: Marcus predicted that most people will not notice when LLMs, especially always-on AI gadgets, persuade them. He set no deadline. The Naaman co-authored study he cites found that most participants in a lab writing task did not notice the AI's influence. A 2026 preregistered experiment also found that most participants missed LLM commercial steering. A 2024 experiment found the opposite: about 61% of participants detected the steering. All of these are short lab tasks. None measures what most people experience with LLM assistants in real-world use. No decisive dated event has settled the forecast, so it stays open.
limitations: Lab studies cannot stand in for a population-wide forecast.
The claim's rhetorical wording ('won't know what hit them') leaves room for interpretation.
The search was limited and may have missed newer field studies.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: once LLM systems, especially always-on wearable assistants, are widely used to persuade people, a majority of the people persuaded will not realize they are being persuaded or manipulated.

The claim looks ahead to a future world of widely used LLM gadgets. Lab studies from before or after the post are consistent with it, or cut against it, but they do not settle a forecast about what most people will experience.
No deadline is stated, so it can only be settled early by a decisive event.
criteria.support_condition: Representative real-world evidence, such as a large field study or official investigation of deployed LLM assistants or wearables, showing that a majority of people who were persuaded or manipulated by them did not notice the influence.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative real-world evidence showing that a majority of people exposed to persuasion by deployed LLM assistants do notice the influence or recognize when they are being steered.

evidence.locator: Section 4.4, 'Were participants aware of the model's opinion and influence?'
evidence.publisher: CHI 2023 (arXiv preprint), Jakesch, Bhat, Buschek, Zalmanson, Naaman
evidence.explanation: The cited study supports the premise. In a lab writing task, most participants did not notice the AI's influence. It comes from before the post and is limited to one task, so it cannot settle the forecast.

evidence.excerpt: LLM-driven persuasion nearly triples the rate at which users select sponsored products compared to traditional search placement (61.2% vs. 22.4%), while the vast majority of participants fail to detect any promotional steering.
evidence.explanation: A later preregistered experiment (N=2,012) found that most participants did not detect LLM steering. This fits the claim, but it is a lab task, not evidence about most people in real-world use.

evidence.excerpt: While around 61% of participants detected the steering attempt by the LLM, a sizeable share of 39% did not.
evidence.explanation: In this consumer-steering experiment, a majority did detect the LLM's steering. That cuts against 'most people won't know', at least in some settings.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A representative field study, regulator investigation, or independent audit of deployed LLM assistants or wearables, measuring whether a majority of exposed users noticed persuasion or steering.
